content: The iodine clock reaction, also known as the Landolt reaction, is a classical chemical clock experiment that demonstrates chemical kinetics in action. It was first discovered in 1886. In this reaction, two clear solutions are mixed together. Initially, there is no visible reaction, but after a short delay, the liquid suddenly changes to a dark blue color. There are several variations of the iodine clock reaction, each involving different chemical components and mechanisms. Hydrogen Peroxide Variation This variation begins with a solution of hydrogen peroxide mixed with sulfuric acid. To this, a second solution containing potassium iodide, sodium thiosulfate, and starch is added. Two distinct reactions occur within the solution. After a certain period, the solution undergoes a rapid color change to a very dark blue, almost black. When the solutions are mixed, the second reaction consumes the triiodide ion at a faster rate than it is produced, maintaining only a small amount of triiodide in dynamic equilibrium. Once the thiosulfate ions are completely consumed, this reaction ceases, and the blue color appears due to the formation of the triiodide-starch complex. Factors that accelerate the first reaction, such as increasing the pH, or the concentration of iodide or hydrogen peroxide, will shorten the time it takes for the solution to change color. Conversely, adding more thiosulfate will delay the appearance of the blue color. Iodate Variation In this alternative protocol, a solution of iodate ions (e.g., potassium iodate) is used. An acidified solution of sodium bisulfite, typically with sulfuric acid, is added to the iodate solution. In this variation, iodide ions are generated through a slow reaction between iodate and bisulfite. This step is the rate-determining step of the reaction. The iodide ions then react with iodine to form the dark blue starch-iodine complex. The reaction dynamics differ from the hydrogen peroxide variation, as the iodide generation is a critical step in this protocol. Persulfate/Peroxydisulfate Variation This version of the iodine clock reaction uses sodium, potassium, or ammonium persulfate to oxidize iodide ions into iodine. Sodium thiosulfate is added to reduce iodine back to iodide before it can form a complex with starch. Once all the thiosulfate is consumed, iodine reacts with starch to produce the characteristic blue-black color. Potassium persulfate has a lower solubility, as noted in documentation from the Salters website, while ammonium persulfate, which has higher solubility, is often used in examples provided by Oxford University. Chlorate Variation An experimental iodine clock sequence has also been developed using a system consisting of iodine, potassium iodide, sodium chlorate, and perchloric acid. This reaction proceeds through a series of steps. In this variation, the induction period refers to the time required for an autocatalytic process to begin. After this induction period, the concentration of free iodine decreases rapidly, as observed through UV/Vis spectroscopy. This variation highlights the role of autocatalysis in the reaction mechanism.
